content: This review is part of a series of six Cochrane reviews that evaluate primary medical treatment options for chronic rhinosinusitis. Chronic rhinosinusitis is a prevalent condition characterized by inflammation of the nasal and paranasal sinus linings. It manifests with symptoms such as nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, facial pain or pressure, and a diminished sense of smell. The condition may present with or without nasal polyps. Oral corticosteroids are often employed to modulate the inflammatory response and alleviate symptoms. The objective of this review was to determine the effects of a short course of oral corticosteroids as an adjunctive therapy in individuals with chronic rhinosinusitis who are already receiving standard treatments. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared short courses (up to 21 days) of oral corticosteroids to placebo or no additional treatment, with all participants concurrently undergoing pharmacological treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis. Two trials, encompassing a total of 78 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The populations studied and the standard treatments provided differed between the two trials. Oral corticosteroids as an adjunct to intranasal corticosteroids: One trial involved 30 adult participants with nasal polyps. All participants were treated with intranasal corticosteroids and were randomized to receive either a short course of oral corticosteroids (oral methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg, tapered over 21 days) or no additional treatment. The study did not report on the primary outcomes of interest, such as disease-specific quality of life or patient-reported disease severity. However, there appeared to be a significant reduction in the size of nasal polyps, as measured by the nasal polyp score (a secondary outcome). The mean difference (MD) was -0.46 (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.87 to -0.05) on a scale of 1 to 4, favoring the group receiving oral corticosteroids. This corresponds to a large effect size, but the evidence is highly uncertain due to the high risk of bias in the study. Additionally, no long-term data or other outcomes of interest were reported. Oral corticosteroids as an adjunct to antibiotics: The second trial included 48 children (mean age of 8 years) without nasal polyps. Participants were randomized to receive either oral corticosteroids (oral methylprednisolone, 1 mg/kg, tapered over 15 days) or placebo, in addition to a 30-day course of antibiotics. This study assessed one primary outcome (disease severity) and one secondary outcome (CT scan score). Disease severity was evaluated using a composite score of four key symptoms in children with chronic rhinosinusitis: nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, facial pressure, and cough. Thirty days after treatment initiation, there was a greater improvement in symptom severity in the group receiving oral corticosteroids and antibiotics compared to the placebo and antibiotics group (MD -7.10, 95% CI -9.59 to -4.61; 45 participants; scale 0 to 40). This represents a large effect size. At the same time point, there was also a significant improvement in CT scan scores in the corticosteroid group (MD -2.90, 95% CI -4.91 to -0.89; 45 participants; scale 0 to 24). However, the quality of the evidence was rated as low. No data were available for longer-term outcomes (e.g., three months post-treatment). Conclusions: The use of oral corticosteroids as an adjunctive therapy to intranasal corticosteroids or antibiotics may lead to improvements in symptom severity, nasal polyp size, and sinus condition as assessed by CT scans. However, the quality of the evidence supporting these findings is low or very low, and the true effect may differ substantially from the reported estimates. It remains unclear whether the benefits of oral corticosteroids are sustained beyond the short follow-up period (up to 30 days), as no long-term data were available. Furthermore, this review did not provide information on the adverse effects associated with short courses of oral corticosteroids. Additional research, particularly studies evaluating long-term outcomes and potential adverse effects, is necessary.
